To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the idea that individuals control their time, and that time is personal, is not normal in Shakespeare.
the idea that time belongs to the self is not normal and that Shakespeare’s drama does not circulate this idea.

Shakespearean characters’ experiences of time, as well as their ability to regulate time, are shaped by social expectations and that Shakespearean drama stages the relationship between personal and social time.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the following questions: How did early modern drama depict and regulate the experience of time?
how Shakespeare’s plays represent the self as a time manager, a self-regulated entity that is able to manage its own time and, as a consequence, to regulate itself.
the following questions: How does Shakespeare’s drama represent and stage the relationship between personal temporal experience and social norms of time?
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
, for Shakespeare, time’s subjectivity is not an exclusively private matter, and the individual’s ability to regulate time is not an exclusively individual matter.
Shakespeare’s drama stages the social and the personal, the public and the individual, as mutually constitutive.
Shakespearean drama stages the individual’s experience of time as a social phenomenon.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
Shakespeare’s drama is not simply about individual time, but about the social norms that shape the individual’s relationship with time.

we have found that Shakespeare’s drama stages the idea of personal time as a social norm, and that it does so through a complex set of social and political expectations that we have identified in his drama.
Shakespeare’s plays stage the social norms and expectations that shape individual time.
The main takeaway from our work is that
Shakespeare’s drama stages a tension between the idea of individual time and the larger social forces that shape that idea.
Shakespeare’s drama stages a variety of social and cultural pressures on time, and that the self is never fully autonomous from these pressures, nor can it ever fully escape them.
Shakespeare’s drama stages the relationship between personal time and its regulation by social norms.
